extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of architecture; architectural critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and criteria for recognizing Gothic buildings and for deciding whether a Gothic building is good architecture, with examples drawn from Venetian, Veronese, and French examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-Gothic vs Linear-Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasting architectural principles: one (Surface-Gothic) attracts the eye to broad sculptured surfaces and strong masses; the other (Linear-Gothic) attracts the eye to involutions of intricate lines and repeated traceries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface-Gothic (illustrated by Veronese examples) confines foliation to certain bearing arches and uses bossy sculpture on broad marble surfaces; Linear-Gothic (illustrated by late French/Abbeville examples) depends on multiplications of similar lines of tracery so that surfaces are almost like lace. Use direct comparison of details (e.g., gable treatments, pinnacles, and mouldings) to classify a building into one of these schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masonry strength, mass, and variety as measures of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Good (Italian/Veronese) Gothic is characterized by strong masonry, simple masses, and perpetual variety; late French Gothic tends to be weak in masonry, broken in mass, and repetitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the building's construction is massive and solid (favoring permanence) and whether its variety is intrinsic; a repeated single idea or excessive foliation indicates a degraded or less noble school even if it is beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: nothing removable without harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition from which anything can be removed without doing mischief is always so far inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether decorative or structural elements are essential to the whole; if key parts can be removed with no deterioration of effect, the work is compositionally weak. Example: removing floral ornaments and statue from a Veronese niche would leave it valueless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof form: steep gable roof
rubrics_metrics.description: First test for Gothic: the roof should rise in a steep gable high above the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the roof does not rise in a steep gable, the building is not pure Gothic or has been altered. Presence of a steep gable combined with other features strongly indicates Gothic of a fine time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arches with gables over principal openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal windows and doors should have pointed arches, and those openings should have gables above them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the main openings are not pointed arches, the building is not Gothic; if they lack gables, it is either impure or not first-rate Gothic. The combination of steep roof, pointed arch, and gable together makes a strong case for a fine Gothic building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusped arches or foliated apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic buildings should exhibit cusped arches or foliated apertures (foliation of traceries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the building meets the first two conditions it will almost certainly have foliation somewhere; absence of foliation indicates imperfect Gothic. Exceptions: large bearing arches or small sharp grouped arches that form foliation by multiplicity and are relieved by sculpture and rich mouldings.

rubrics_metrics.name: True shafts with bases and capitals at arch springs
rubrics_metrics.description: Arches (windows, doors, minor ornamentation) should be carried on true shafts with bases and capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If shafts and capitals are present, the building is of the finest Gothic style. If apertures are plain openings without moulding, the building may still be fine (domestic/military adaptation). But moulded sides without capitals indicate an inferior school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of construction by 'strong men' (character of workmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good architecture shows roughness, largeness, nonchalance, and occasional exquisite tenderness — signs of masterful builders who 'see past' their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very accurate, minute, scrupulous workmanship is suspicious: it may indicate either the very best (conscientious design) or the very worst (mechanism replacing design); in practice, excessive precision often signals an inferior school. Prefer expressive strength over mere mechanical neatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularity and parts fitting their purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A good building will show purposeful irregularities: parts fitting to different purposes rather than mechanical symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different elements answer different practical needs and the composition accommodates them (e.g., slightly offset windows or uneven arcs), this irregularity is a sign of a masterful design; perfect, predictable correspondence of parts tends to indicate a later or inferior building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual variety in traceries, capitals, and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: All traceries, capitals, and other ornaments should exhibit continually varied design rather than repetitive patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unique and varied details across the building; repetition or uniformity in ornamentation is evidence of comparative lateness or inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and scale of sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture on a good building is arranged and scaled so that it is intelligible and interesting at ordinary viewing distance; upper sculptures are often colossal (10–12 feet) with ornament increasing in fineness toward the foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that sculptural groups and statues are legible from the typical vantage point and that there is a considered gradation of scale (large/colossal high up, finer detail near the eye). If sculpture is illegible, the historical or artistic value is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of ornament as a dating/detail criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In earlier (transitional/Byzantine-influenced) palaces, ornamentation is centralized (central capital/central sculpture made superior); later buildings (e.g. Ducal Palace) abandon this subtle centralization and use ungroped or all-different capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine groups of windows: if the midmost capital is distinct and the lateral ones answer each other, the group is likely anterior to the Ducal Palace; uniform or all-different capitals suggest a later date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceries as structural support in Venetian Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: In Venetian Gothic the traceries often support actual building loads (not merely glass), so ponderous traceries indicate a light internal structure relying on traceries for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate traceries not just as decoration but as structural elements: heavy traceries that bear weight imply a design economy (strength with minimal material). Contrast with Northern Gothic where traceries primarily support glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic palace general form: arcades break into centralized windows and doors
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces tend to break Byzantine continuous arcades into distinct central and lateral windows and small arched doors; the sea-story changes from continuous arches to a central door with flanking windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the shift from long continuous arcade composition to a composition with a central emphasis (door or middle light) and lateral windows. This reorganization of façade elements is characteristic of Gothic palaces and reflects functional/domestic adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic detailing: string-courses, chamfered angles, and twisted shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic palaces display boldly projecting and decorated string-courses between stories, chamfered angles filled with small twisted shafts, and other details that convey lightness and assurance of stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for these recurring practical details (e.g., chamfered angles with twisted pillars divided by bands, projecting string-courses, marble facings changed to brick or stucco) as diagnostic features of Venetian Gothic palaces and as means by which builders conveyed structural confidence.
